When the code changes: retrieval failure across India's 2024 statutory recodification

Udita Uniyal · Banasthali Vidyapith · 3 September 2026 · commit b720937

A report on a legal question-answering system, what was measured in it, and what those measurements mean. Written for a reader with no prior exposure to this project. Every technical term is defined in Appendix A.

No number in this report was typed by hand. Each one is extracted from a results file by a filter that must match exactly one row or the program stops. The full ledger — every value with its confidence interval, sample size and regenerating command — is Appendix B.

1 · The six sentences

If you read nothing else, read these. There are no numbers in them, because the findings do not depend on the numbers being memorised.

  1. A system searching Indian criminal law finds the repealed code far more reliably than the code actually in force.
  2. Switching from meaning-based search to keyword search does not fix this — it breaks the opposite half, and combining the two is worse than either.
  3. The cause lies in how statutes are written: the new code names itself in its own text, the old one never did, so the old code's name now belongs to a different book.
  4. The system's own confidence score is worse at telling right from wrong than a simpler number it already had for free, and correcting a genuine bug inside it does not close the gap.
  5. There is no confidence setting at which the system can answer some questions and be reliably right about them.
  6. None of this is visible in the answers the system writes, because the language model cites correct law regardless of what the search found.

2 · The problem

India replaced three law books in one day

On 1 July 2024 India replaced its colonial-era criminal statutes. What counts as a crime moved from the Indian Penal Code of 1860 to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita of 2023. Arrest, bail and trial procedure moved from the Code of Criminal Procedure to the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita. Evidence moved from the Indian Evidence Act to the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam.

Same offences. Different section numbers.

Why this is genuinely hard, not merely inconvenient

Both books remain live law. Which one applies depends on when the conduct happened, not on when the question is asked. Old law is preserved for old conduct by savings provisions and by section 6 of the General Clauses Act 1897. Article 20(1) of the Constitution separately forbids applying a heavier punishment retrospectively.

That produces a situation with no equivalent in ordinary document search:

> "My husband beats me — this happened in March 2023." The answer is > IPC 498A. > > "My husband beats me — this happened last month." The answer is > BNS 85. > > Identical words. Only the date decides.

And it is not simple renumbering. IPC 379, theft, became BNS 303(2) — which also adds community service for a first offence under five thousand rupees. A system that merely swaps numbers is still wrong about the law.

Why it matters

Someone typing "my husband beats me" does not know the Indian Penal Code exists, let alone that it was replaced last year. They will not supply a date. Yet the section number they are handed is the one that goes on their police complaint.

That is the gap this project measures: between what a person can be expected to say, and what the system needs in order to be right.

3 · Where this began, and what changed

The system that already existed

This project did not start from nothing. A working five-agent pipeline was built and documented before any of the measurement in this report took place. That document described the architecture reproduced in section 4: intake, routing, retrieval, answering, reporting.

It named one component as the project's principal contribution — the composite confidence score. Three signals combined by fixed weights: the average similarity of the best five retrieved passages at 55%, a penalty for uneven scores at 15%, and a check for whether those passages contain section numbers named in the question at 30%. Three confidence tiers followed from it, and the tiers changed the system's behaviour: which warning was attached to the answer, which passages reached the model, what colour badge the user saw.

It also stated three design principles as achieved properties: that answers are grounded, with every claim traceable to a stored passage; that the system refuses rather than hallucinating when retrieval fails; and that routing is deterministic and therefore free of routing errors.

What that evidence could and could not support

The evidence was two queries.

Not two hundred. Two — chosen by hand, examined after the fact, with no record of what the correct answer should have been. Nobody had written down in advance which statutory section each question ought to retrieve, so there was nothing for the system to be right or wrong against. And no retrieval score had ever been written to disk, so the two numbers reported could not be recomputed even in principle.

Both of those are ordinary for an architecture document. Neither is sufficient for a claim about how well a system performs.

One of the two worked examples reproduces exactly; the other does not. This is checkable by hand from the formula that document states.

The first reported a top-five mean of 0.499, a score gap of 0.037, and entity coverage of 1.00, giving 70.6%. Working it through: the first term is 0.55 × 0.499 = 0.2745. The gap penalty is 0.037 ÷ 0.3 = 0.123, so the second term is 0.15 × (1 − 0.123) = 0.1315. The third is 0.30 × 1.00 = 0.30. They sum to 0.7060. Exact.

The second reported 43.3%, with a top-five mean of about 0.40, a score gap described as "Small", and entity coverage described as "Low". Entity coverage is a count of matching passages divided by a count of entities, so with the two entities in that query it can only take values such as 0, 0.5 or 1.0 — nothing in between. Taking 0.5, reaching 43.3% requires the gap term to contribute 0.063, which needs a score gap of roughly 0.17. On a scale where 0.3 is the maximum, 0.17 is not small. The row contradicts its own description, and it should not be carried into any paper.

The same document already contained the evidence of a defect nobody had noticed. Its corpus table lists the Indian Penal Code tagged as BNS, and the Code of Criminal Procedure tagged as BNSS. Both tags are wrong, and they are wrong in exactly the direction that matters here: the repealed statute labelled as the one that replaced it. The corpus-tagging defect that later measurement confirmed was sitting in the original documentation, in a table, unremarked.

The pivot

The work described in this report began by changing the question.

The original question was does the system work? Two examples cannot answer that. The replacement question was what does it get wrong, and why? Two examples cannot answer that either — but a properly constructed evaluation set can, and that is what section 5 describes building.

Three things followed from the change.

The confidence score changed role. It stopped being the contribution and became the object of study. Finding 6.4 reports what measuring it produced, and the result is negative — which is a contribution of a different and more durable kind than the one originally claimed.

The recodification changed role. In the original document the coexistence of the old and new criminal codes is background, a fact about the corpus. Here it is the subject. The cross-statute failure is not a defect found along the way; it is the phenomenon being studied.

The routing bug changed role. Under the first framing it is an embarrassment to be fixed quietly. Under the second it is data.

What was added to the architecture

The pipeline in section 4 is not the pipeline that was first documented. Two stages were inserted between routing and retrieval, because measurement showed they were needed.

A date resolver reads the question for any indication of when the conduct happened — "last month", "in 2023", an explicit date — and converts it into which legal era governs. A statute mapper then takes the section numbers the router extracted and translates them across the recodification, so that a question naming a repealed section can also be searched for under the section that replaced it.

Both were measured rather than assumed. On the question set where the code named in the question and the date of the conduct disagree — the hard case, and the one a member of the public is most likely to produce — retrieval of the correct section rose from 0.293 [0.212, 0.389] to 0.694 [0.597, 0.776]. The two intervals do not overlap, which means the improvement is larger than sampling noise could explain. It is the largest single gain recorded in this project.

F10 — Adding a date resolver and a statute mapper more than doubled retrieval of the correct section on the hard case: where the question names one code but the conduct falls under the other. The two intervals do not overlap, so the gain is larger than sampling noise could explain.

What did not change is the five-agent structure itself. The pivot was in what was asked of the system, not in rebuilding it. The two new stages were added because a measurement said they were needed, and their effect was then measured in turn.

4 · What was built

A five-stage pipeline. A question in plain English goes in; an answer with citations and a PDF report comes out. Two stages use a language model; the rest are fixed rules or database search.

M1 — The whole system. A question enters at the left and a cited answer with a PDF leaves at the right. Pink boxes use a language model; blue boxes are fixed rules or database search.

The corpus holds 1,899 passages of statutory text. That number matters because every proportion in this report is a share of it, and because it is smaller than the system's original documentation claimed. Four statutes are present: the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 with 742 passages, the Indian Penal Code 1860 with 595, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 with 424, and the Consumer Protection Act 2019 with 138.

Four things the original documentation claimed that are not true, and are not reproduced here. The corpus does not contain the BNSS, the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, the Constitution, or case law — those were never ingested. The refusal mechanism does not protect users, because it has never once triggered. The composite confidence score is not the system's key innovation, because it performs worse than a simpler alternative. And the passage count is not 1,011. Section 7 sets out the full list.

How a question moves through the system

The first stage reads the question and extracts structure from it — what kind of legal problem it is, and what facts are missing.

M2 — The intake stage. It reads the question and extracts structure: what kind of legal problem this is, and which facts are missing.

The second stage decides which law book to search. It works by matching words in the question against a fixed table. Three of its branches point at books that are not in the index at all, marked on the diagram: a question about evidence law is routed to a filter that matches nothing, and the search then silently falls back to searching everything.

M3 — The routing stage, which decides which law book to search by matching words against a fixed table. Three branches point at books that were never ingested and therefore match nothing; the search then silently falls back to searching everything.

The third stage is the retrieval pipeline, and it is where every headline finding in this report is measured. Seven steps: embed the question, search, fall back if needed, reorder, filter by score, score confidence, return.

M4 — The seven retrieval steps. Every headline finding in this report is measured here. Note steps 4 and 5: reranking reorders the fifteen results, and the adaptive filter discards the weakest, which is why a recall figure must always name which of the three stages produced it.

Two of those steps deserve names, because the rest of this report distinguishes them constantly. The corpus filter restricts the search to one statute before it runs. The adaptive score filter discards weak results after. Confusing the two produces meaningless numbers, and earlier versions of this project did exactly that.

The fourth stage writes the answer using only the passages it was given.

M5 — The answer stage. The refusal gate is real code, but it has never triggered in 859 recorded queries, so in practice every question is answered.

Confidence is computed from three signals and used to pick which warning to attach to the answer.

M6 — How confidence is computed: three signals combined by fixed weights. Finding 6.4 shows this combination performs worse than one of its own inputs used alone.

Ingestion, run once, converts PDFs into the indexed passages.

M7 — Ingestion, run once. PDFs become text, text becomes passages, passages become vectors, vectors go into the database.

And the whole path, end to end:

M8a — The same path in time order, first half: the question arrives, is triaged, routed, embedded, and searched against the database. Split in two so the labels stay legible at page width.

M8b — Second half: retrieved passages become a cited answer and a PDF, which return to the user.

5 · How it was measured

Written for someone who has never evaluated a search system.

Why "did it work?" is not one question

Suppose you ask "what is the punishment for cheating under section 420 of the Indian Penal Code?" and the system replies with a correct-sounding paragraph citing IPC 420.

Did it work? There are three different things you might mean.

  • Did the search find the right law? The system fetches fifteen passages

before writing anything. Was IPC 420 among them? This is the question about retrieval, and in this report it is called retrieved@k.

  • Did the answer name the right law? Does IPC 420 appear in the citations?

This is the question about writing, called cited.

  • Was the answer actually supported? Was every section it cited genuinely

present in the passages it was given, or did the model supply some from memory? This is the strict question, called grounded.

These come apart, and finding 6.6 is a case where the answer is yes under one definition and no under another. That is why all three are always reported, and why every number in this report says which one it used.

Why the stage matters too

The fifteen fetched passages pass through three states before the model sees them. They arrive from the database in score order — raw_15. They are reordered to promote passages containing section numbers from the question — reranked_15. Then weak ones are discarded — filtered_n, which is what actually reaches the language model.

A recall figure means a different thing at each. "The right law was found" could mean the database returned it, or that it survived to the model. Earlier versions of this project published figures without recording which, and that single omission made two numbers look like a contradiction when they were both correct. Every figure here names its stage.

The questions used

Four sets, 518 unique questions, each with its correct statutory section recorded before any system output was seen.

The generated set of 198 questions and the paired set of 99 are certain by construction: each was built from a known section, so the section is the answer by definition. The dated-conflict set of 197 and the layman set of 120 required legal judgement — deciding which section governs a described situation — and that judgement was made by one person. Section 8 treats this as the largest threat to everything reported here.

The paired set is the experiment rather than merely the data: it asks the same legal question twice, once with the old code's number and once with the new one's. Any difference between the two arms is attributable to the numbering, because nothing else changed.

How the measurements were checked

Four safeguards, because a metric that returns a plausible wrong number is the failure this project was built to avoid.

237 automated tests, including tests where the correct output was worked out by hand before the code ran. One shared measurement library, imported by every experiment, so no two experiments can disagree about what a word means. A second, independent re-derivation inside each experiment, which recomputes one of its own numbers by a different route and stops if the two disagree. And no manual transcription anywhere: every number in every results document is extracted by a filter that crashes rather than guess if it matches more than one row.

That last safeguard caught two real errors while this report was being written, and both are in section 6.

6 · The findings

Strongest evidence first.

6.1 The system is more reliable on the law that no longer applies

The finding. When a question names the repealed code, the system usually finds the right law. When it names the code actually in force, it finds the right law barely more often than if it had ignored the question entirely.

What this means in practice. A law student researching a 2019 offence gets good results. A citizen asking about something that happened last month — the case where the answer goes on a police complaint — gets results little better than chance.

F2 — Naming the repealed statute works; naming the one in force barely beats chance. Red ticks are the chance baseline: each statute's share of the index, i.e. what a retriever ignoring the question would score.

Questions naming the Indian Penal Code retrieve mostly IPC text 97.0% of the time, and since the IPC occupies 31.3% of the index, that is far above what ignoring the question would achieve. Questions naming the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita retrieve mostly BNS text only 51.5% of the time against a 22.3% baseline — real, but weak. Both rest on 33 questions per arm, so their 95% confidence intervals are wide: [84.7%, 99.5%] and [35.2%, 67.5%]. Narrowing them would need more questions, not better analysis.

The misses do not scatter. When a BNS-named question fails, the passages it gets back are overwhelmingly from the repealed code — the failure has a direction, which is what makes it a finding rather than noise.

The same pattern appears again inside the pipeline. Of every fifteen passages fetched for a layman question, the share coming from the procedure code rises from 1.49 times its fair share to 1.80 times after the weak results are discarded, while the share from the code in force falls from 0.58 to 0.34 times. A step whose only job is removing noise is removing substantive criminal law and concentrating procedure.

F5 — Recall@15 is the share of questions whose correct section was present. The adaptive score filter costs every query set a little and the layman set half of what it had. But the layman line starts at 15%: the filter is not the main problem, the retrieval is. Correctness definition retrieved@k; shaded bands are 95% Wilson intervals.

That filter costs the layman questions half of what they had: recall falls from 0.150 to 0.075. But read the starting point before drawing the wrong conclusion. Even before any filtering, only 0.150 of layman questions had their correct section retrieved at all. Removing the filter entirely would still leave most ordinary-language questions unanswered. The filter is a secondary problem.

How it could be wrong. The measure is coarse: it asks which statute dominates the fifteen passages, which can score zero even when the single best passage is correct — finding 6.2 contains exactly such a case. The corpus filter is switched off for this measurement, because with it on an IPC-named question physically cannot return BNS text, and the question becomes unaskable. And 33 questions per arm is a small sample.

6.2 Keyword search does not fix it; it breaks the other half

The finding. The obvious remedy — search for exact words instead of meaning — fails in the opposite direction, and combining the two methods produces a system that fails at both.

What this means in practice. There is no drop-in retrieval fix. Anyone proposing to solve this by changing the search engine has to explain which half of the queries they are willing to lose.

F3 — Exact-word search does not repair the failure, it reverses it. Fusing the two (green) lands between them and beats neither: averaging two opposite failure modes fails at both.

Keyword search raises accuracy on questions naming the code in force from 51.5% to 97.0% — a large and real improvement. But on questions naming the repealed code it collapses from 97.0% to 0.0%, which is below the 31.3% a system ignoring the question would score. Fusing the two methods lands in between on both arms, at 45.5% and 78.8%, and beats neither at what it was good at. Averaging two opposite failures gives you a system that fails twice.

How it could be wrong. The 0.0% figure is an artefact of the coarse measure. On at least one question, keyword search puts the correct IPC section first and then fills the remaining fourteen slots with procedure-code cross-references, so "which statute dominates" scores it zero. Judged on the single best passage instead, keyword search is not catastrophic. The direction of the finding survives; the magnitude is exaggerated.

6.3 The cause is in how the statutes are written

The finding. The new code writes its own name inside its own text. The old one never did. So the old code's name has become, statistically, a word belonging to a different book.

What this means in practice. This is not a bug anyone introduced and not something a better search engine fixes. It is a property of legal drafting, and it should recur in any jurisdiction that replaces a statute rather than amending it.

F4 — Bars are coloured by the statute the term concentrates in (green BNS/CPA, red CrPC, grey mixed). 'sanhita' occurs in 30 chunks, all BNS — a perfect signpost. 'penal' occurs in 110, but 82 are CrPC and only 23 are IPC: the Penal Code's own name points elsewhere.

The word sanhita appears in 30 of the 1,899 passages, and every single one is Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita text. A search for it lands in the right book every time — it is a perfect signpost.

The word penal appears in 110 passages. Only 23 are Indian Penal Code. 82 are Code of Criminal Procedure. Searching for the Penal Code by its own name points at the procedure code roughly three times more often than at the Penal Code itself.

The reason is mundane once seen. The 1860 drafters had no occasion to write "penal" inside the Penal Code; you do not name the book you are in. The procedure code, by contrast, cites it constantly, because procedure refers to offences. So the old statute's name survives mainly in the documents that mention it, not in the document that is it.

Both statutes name themselves rarely — the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 7.1% [5.0%, 9.9%] of its own passages, the Indian Penal Code in 3.9% [2.6%, 5.7%]. The asymmetry that matters is not how often they say their names, but whether saying the name identifies the book.

How it could be wrong. Only presence was counted, not how many times a word occurs within a passage; keyword search uses both, so this explains the direction of the effect without fully reconstructing the ranking. The corpus is four statutes, and the argument that this generalises is an argument, not a measurement.

6.4 The confidence score is worse than a number it already had

The finding. The system combines three signals into a confidence score. That combination separates right answers from wrong ones less well than the single simplest number available, and fixing a genuine bug inside it does not close the gap.

What this means in practice. The engineering effort that went into the composite score bought nothing. Anyone building on this system should use the raw similarity and spend the effort elsewhere.

F6 — The deployed composite (red) is beaten by three of its own ingredients. One term is inverted and scores below chance. Correcting the sign lifts the blend (blue) but it still loses to a single raw similarity (green). Measured under correctness definition retrieved@k at retrieval stage raw_15.

The measure is AUROC: pick one right answer and one wrong answer at random, and ask how often the right one scored higher. Half means the score is a coin flip.

The deployed composite scores 0.6631 [0.6172, 0.7096]. The single highest similarity from the search — a number already sitting in the logs, costing nothing — scores 0.7837 [0.7470, 0.8195]. Two of the composite's own three ingredients also beat it: 0.7571 and 0.7298. A blend of three signals is worse than one of the signals alone.

One ingredient turned out to be wired backwards. The gap between the best and second-best result is evidence of a clear winner, but the deployed code treats it as evidence of doubt, and measured on its own that inverted term scores 0.2702 — below half, meaning it points the wrong way.

That raised an obvious objection: perhaps the whole finding is just this bug. It is not. Correcting the sign lifts the composite to 0.7207, a real improvement, but it still loses to the simple number by -0.0630 [-0.0946, -0.0325]. The bug explains about half of the original -0.1207 shortfall; the rest is the blend itself. And when the three corrected signals are given the best weighting that can be found, then tested on questions the search never saw, they reach 0.7631 — a tie with the simple number, never a win.

One thing does work, in one place. A fourth signal was built for this project: the fraction of retrieved passages that come from the statute the question and its date imply. Overall it scores 0.6845 [0.6557, 0.7139], no better than what already existed. But on the 197 questions where the named code and the offence date disagree — precisely the hard case — it reaches 0.8300 [0.7819, 0.8750]. The catch is that on most other questions the search filter was itself built from the same date information, so the signal cannot fail there by construction. It earns its keep only where the question and the date pull apart.

How it could be wrong. Under the strict grounded definition there are only 27 right answers among 617 questions, and every comparison under it is too underpowered to separate anything. This finding rests on the other two definitions.

6.5 There is no confidence setting that makes the system safe

The finding. The standard safety mechanism for a system like this is to answer only when confident and stay silent otherwise. These measurements say that mechanism cannot be built on the current confidence score.

What this means in practice. You cannot deploy this behind a rule like "only answer when at least 90% likely to be right", because no such threshold exists at any level of caution.

F8 — Under retrieved@k, BOTH scores are at or near zero: there is no confidence threshold at which the system can answer any share of questions and be wrong only one time in ten. These zeros are measured, not missing. The full risk-coverage curve is not in the results files and is not shown.

If the system answered only its most confident questions, what share could it answer while being wrong at most one time in ten? For the composite score the answer is 0.0000 — no threshold anywhere on the curve reaches that error rate. For the simple similarity score it is 0.0486. These zeros are measured values, not missing data.

F7 — On the diagonal means a claimed confidence matches observed accuracy. The deployed composite (red) is NON-MONOTONE: it peaks in the middle and falls back at the top, so its most confident answers are no better than its middling ones. max_score (green) rises throughout.

The reason is visible in the shape of the curve. A well-behaved confidence score climbs steadily: the more confident it is, the more often it is right. The composite does not. It rises through the middle of its range and then falls back at the top, so the answers it is most sure about are no better than its middling ones. The simple similarity score climbs throughout.

A summary statistic hides this completely. The composite's calibration error is 0.2410 [0.2016, 0.2695] against 0.1270 [0.1065, 0.1681] for the simple score — worse, but a single number cannot tell you that the curve bends the wrong way at the end, which is the part that matters for safety.

How it could be wrong. The composite was never designed to be a probability; it is a weighted sum of similarity scores. Calibration measures assume a probability, so applying them here needs the caveat. The zeros are a real property of this score, not proof that no score could work.

6.6 None of this shows up in the answers

The finding. The retrieval failure is invisible in what the system writes, because the language model cites correct sections whether or not the search found them.

What this means in practice. Anyone evaluating this system by reading its answers would conclude it works. The failure is only visible if you inspect what was retrieved — and a legal system whose failures are invisible is more dangerous than one whose failures are obvious.

The gap between the two arms of the paired set is 0.5455 [0.3030, 0.7576] when measured on what was retrieved — a large, clear difference. Measured on what was cited it is -0.0303 [-0.1212, 0.0606], an interval straddling zero, which means the data cannot distinguish the two arms at all. Under the strict definition it is -0.0303 [-0.0909, 0.0000], again straddling zero.

The mechanism is straightforward and was measured directly: the arm asking with old-code numbering cites the correct section about nine times in ten, and the arm asking with new-code numbering does about as well. The model supplies correct citations from its own training regardless of what the search returned.

How it could be wrong. This is stated throughout as a claim about retrieval. A reviewer who measures citation accuracy instead will not reproduce the headline gap, and would be right not to. The finding is that the two disagree — which is why every number in this report names its definition.

8 · Limitations

Stated as a reviewer would state them.

  1. All ground truth was decided by one person. Two of the four question sets required legal judgement about which section governs a described situation. No independent expert has validated any label. This is the largest threat to every finding in this report.
  2. A ceiling caps every retrieval figure. Only 85.7% [82.4%, 88.5%] of 518 questions have a correct answer the index can return at all, because some gold labels name a subsection stored only as a whole section. On questions naming the code in force the ceiling is 33.3%. Recall figures must be read against this, not against 100% — and on that subset the retrieval that was measured reaches the ceiling exactly, meaning it is perfect on everything reachable.

F9 — Where gold labels name a subsection the index stores only as a bare section, no retriever can score them. BNS-named queries are capped at 33.3%: every recall figure must be read against this, not against 100%.

  1. One embedding model, one vector database, one jurisdiction, four statutes. No result generalises beyond this configuration without retesting.
  2. The strict correctness definition is underpowered, with 27 right answers among 617 questions. Every comparison under it straddles zero.
  3. One significance claim is lost under proper clustering. Three phrasings of one situation are not three independent facts. The layman retrieval rate after filtering is significant when rows are treated as independent [0.033, 0.125] and not significant when situations are [0.000, 0.167], because the successes concentrate in a few situations.
  4. One verification assertion is left deliberately failing. Four clustered intervals came out narrower than their unclustered counterparts and remain unexplained after ruling out implementation bugs and random variation across five seeds. Those two subsets are marked unusable rather than explained away.
  5. Three labelled rows are dropped by a deduplication rule, so the sample is 617 where it could be 620. Disclosed rather than fixed, because changing it would shift every number in ten results files for a difference that moves no conclusion.
  6. The headline finding is definition-dependent and does not survive at citation level, as section 6.6 states.
  7. Answer quality was not evaluated. This work measures retrieval, confidence and citation behaviour. It does not assess whether the legal advice is sound.

Appendix A · Glossary

Every technical term used in this report, in plain language.

adaptive score filter — A step that discards retrieved passages scoring below a threshold set from the best score in that search. Distinct from the corpus filter, which restricts the search before it runs.

AUROC — Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve. Pick one correct answer and one wrong answer at random; AUROC is the probability the correct one has the higher score. 0.5 is a coin flip and means the score knows nothing; 1.0 is perfect separation; below 0.5 means the score points the wrong way.

BM25 — A search method that ranks documents by which query words literally appear in them, weighted by how often and how rare each word is. Contrast with dense retrieval, which matches on meaning rather than exact words.

BNS — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023. India's criminal code since 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code.

BNSS — Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023. The new criminal procedure code. NOT in this system's corpus.

bootstrap confidence interval — A range computed by resampling the data many times (here 10,000) and seeing how much the answer moves. It says: given this sample size, the true value plausibly lies in this range.

Brier score — The average squared difference between a claimed probability and what actually happened. Lower is better; 0 is perfect. Claiming 0.9 on something that happens costs (1−0.9)² = 0.01.

calibration — Whether a stated confidence matches reality. A perfectly calibrated system that says '70% confident' is right 70 times in 100.

chunk — One passage of statutory text stored in the database, typically a section or part of one. This corpus holds 1,899 of them.

cluster bootstrap — A confidence interval that resamples GROUPS rather than rows. Three phrasings of the same legal situation are not three independent facts; treating them as such makes intervals look narrower than they are.

corpus filter — A restriction applied BEFORE searching, limiting the search to one statute. Distinct from the adaptive score filter, which drops low-scoring passages afterwards. Conflating the two is a common error here.

coverage at risk — If you answered only the questions you were most confident about, what share could you answer while keeping errors at or below some level (here 10%)?

CPA — Consumer Protection Act 2019.

CrPC — Code of Criminal Procedure 1973. Still in this corpus; replaced in law by the BNSS.

dense retrieval — Search by meaning. Each passage and each question becomes a list of 1,536 numbers (an embedding); similar meanings give similar lists.

ECE — Expected Calibration Error. Sort answers by confidence, group them into bins, and average how far each bin's claimed confidence sits from its actual accuracy. Lower is better; 0 is perfect.

embedding — A list of numbers representing a piece of text's meaning. Here 1,536 numbers produced by openai/text-embedding-3-small.

entity coverage — One of the system's three confidence signals: whether section numbers named in the question appear in the retrieved passages.

gold label — See ground truth.

ground truth — The correct answer, decided in advance by a human and recorded before any system output was seen. Here: which statutory section correctly answers each query.

IDF — Inverse Document Frequency. How informative a word is, from how few documents contain it. A word in 30 of 1,899 chunks is a strong clue; a word in 1,500 tells you almost nothing.

IPC — Indian Penal Code 1860. Repealed on 1 July 2024 but still governing any offence committed before that date.

lexical retrieval — Search by exact words rather than meaning. BM25 is the lexical method used here.

MRR — Mean Reciprocal Rank. If the correct passage is at position 1 you score 1, at position 2 you score 1/2, at position 4 you score 1/4. Averaged over all queries. Rewards putting the right answer near the top.

nDCG — Normalised Discounted Cumulative Gain. Like MRR, a rank-sensitive score that penalises correct answers appearing further down the list.

p-value — The probability of seeing a difference at least this large if there were really no difference at all. Small means the difference is unlikely to be chance alone. It does NOT say how big or how important the difference is.

paired test — A comparison that uses the fact that two scores were measured on the SAME questions. Comparing two separate confidence intervals by eye is not a test and is far too conservative.

precision@k — Of the k passages returned, what share are correct. With a single correct section per query it equals recall@k divided by k, so it adds no information here and is reported only for completeness.

Qdrant — The vector database storing the 1,899 embedded passages and answering nearest-neighbour searches over them.

RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Fetch relevant documents first, then have a language model write an answer using only those documents. The idea is that the model quotes sources rather than inventing them.

reachability ceiling — The highest score any retriever could possibly achieve, given that some correct answers are not stored in a form the system can return. Scores must be read against this, not against 100%.

recall@k — Of the questions that have a correct section, the share where that section appeared among the top k retrieved passages. The central retrieval measure in this report.

reciprocal rank fusion — A way of combining two ranked lists: each document scores 1/(60 + its rank) in each list, and the scores are added. The constant 60 is from Cormack, Clarke and Buttcher, SIGIR 2009.

recodification — Replacing a statute wholesale with a new one rather than amending it. India replaced the Indian Penal Code 1860 with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 on 1 July 2024. Both remain operative: which applies depends on when the offence occurred.

reliability diagram — A plot of claimed confidence against observed accuracy. A perfectly calibrated system sits on the diagonal.

risk-coverage curve — As you accept lower-confidence answers, coverage rises and so does error. The curve traces that trade-off.

savings provision — A clause keeping an old law alive for conduct that happened while it was in force, even after repeal. This is why both India's old and new criminal codes are simultaneously live law.

score gap — One of the three confidence signals: the difference between the best and second-best retrieval score. A large gap suggests a clear winner.

self-naming — Whether a statute writes its own name inside its own text. It determines whether searching for a statute by name finds it.

statute consistency — A fourth confidence signal, specified in the design and built for the first time in this work: the fraction of retrieved passages coming from the statute the question and its date imply.

top-k mean — One of the three confidence signals: the average similarity of the top few retrieved passages.
